newsitem.title: BRAZIL: SOCCER-RIO BEGINS YEAR WITH TRADITIONAL CHAOS.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-RIO BEGINS YEAR WITH TRADITIONAL CHAOS.

text.p: Three of Rio de Janeiro's four leading clubs have threatened to boycott this year's state championship because they don't agree with the rules of the competition.

In a row that has almost become a part of local soccer tradition, Flamengo, Fluminense and Botafogo said they would walk out on the tournament unless the Rio de Janeiro federation backed down on a decision made on Monday to change the rules.
"This state championship is financial suicide," said Flamengo director Michel Assef on Thursday, referring to the new set of rules. "We will not accept this formula under any circumstances."

Originally, the federation had agreed a somewhat strange formula under which the 12 clubs would take part in the first stage with the major four -- Flamengo, Fluminense, Botafogo and Vasco da Gama -- automatically going into the second stage. They would be joined by the best four of the remaining clubs. The second stage would then have been contested on a straightforward round-robin basis.
Under the new rules, approved at a meeting on Monday, the winners of the first stage will meet the winners of the second stage in a final which will decide the competition.
Under the original option, the first stage would have been merely academic for the major clubs.

But this suited Flamengo, Fluminense and Botafogo, who had planned to field junior teams and send their first-choice squads to play in a more lucrative Rio-Sao Paulo tournament and friendlies around the country.
Arguments over the formula of the competition, which varies from year to year, take place almost annually.
The formulas are decided at rowdy meetings which frequently turn into battles between an alliance of Vasco and the smaller clubs on one hand and Flamengo, Fluminense and Botafogo on the other.
Brazil is the only major country to hold regional championships, which take place in the first half of the year. The Brazilian championship itself lasts for just four months.
There has been criticism of the system for years, with the major sides complaining that the regional championships force them into too many loss-making fixtures against minor sides.
